analysis.one_liner: Requires independent audits and anti-discrimination rules for AI systems used in major life decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to use an algorithm in a way that discriminates by race, sex, disability, income, and other protected traits in decisions that shape people's lives — hiring, housing, credit, insurance, health care, benefits, policing, and elections. Companies would have to test their algorithms for bias before launch through independent auditors, check for harms every year, tell people in plain language (and in the ten most common US languages) how the systems are used, and give people the right to a human decision and an appeal. Enforcement would sit with the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals, who could sue — even overriding forced-arbitration clauses — with penalties up to $15,000 per violation or treble damages.
analysis.who_benefits: People on the receiving end of algorithmic decisions: job applicants and workers evaluated by software, renters and homebuyers scored by landlords and lenders, insurance and benefits applicants, patients, people facing predictive policing or risk scores, and voters touched by election-related algorithms. The bill would give them mandatory bias audits they could read, notices in plain language and in the ten most-spoken US languages, a right to opt for a human decision and to appeal an automated one, protection from retaliation, and the ability to sue in court — including overriding pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People judged by algorithms in hiring, housing, credit, policing

how_it_helps.text: Bans developers and deployers from using algorithms that discriminate — including through disparate impact — in employment, housing, credit, insurance, health care, utilities, education, criminal justice, elections, government benefits, and other consequential areas [S2].

Requires a pre-deployment evaluation by an independent auditor (who cannot have a financial stake in the company) before any algorithm is used in a consequential decision, plus an annual impact assessment if harm occurred, with summaries published on a public FTC repository [S2].

Gives individuals a right to opt out of an automated decision and have a human make it, a right to appeal an automated decision to a human, protection from retaliation, and whistleblower protection for employees who report violations [S2].

Creates real enforcement teeth: FTC enforcement (with jurisdiction extended to banks, common carriers, airlines, and nonprofits), state attorney general suits with civil penalties of $15,000 per violation or 4% of annual revenue, and a private right of action with treble damages or $15,000 per violation — and invalidates pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for disputes under the Act [S2].

Requires disclosures in plain language in the ten most common US languages and accessible formats, and builds federal capacity by creating an algorithm-auditing job series and up to 500 new FTC positions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that build or use algorithms in consequential decisions — software and AI developers, employers, lenders, landlords, insurers, health systems, and agencies — would bear audit and compliance costs, litigation exposure from the private right of action, and civil penalties. Taxpayers would fund the new FTC staffing and federal auditor corps, though the bill authorizes rather than appropriates those sums [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: AI developers and companies using automated decisions

drawbacks.text: The scope is extremely broad: a 'covered algorithm' reaches nearly any computational process touching a consequential decision, so audit, documentation, and notice requirements would fall on businesses of every size, and some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers as higher prices [S2].

The private right of action allows treble damages or $15,000 per violation plus attorney's fees, and voids arbitration clauses — which helps victims get to court but also invites litigation volume and defensive compliance behavior from companies [S2].

The bill presumes an independent auditing profession that barely exists at the required scale; auditor independence rules bar anyone with ties to the developer or deployer, which could create bottlenecks, high audit prices, and inconsistent quality [S2].

Enforcement depends heavily on future FTC rulemaking (the definition of a covered algorithm, opt-out rules, and appeal rules are all left to regulations over years), so the protections' real-world strength would hinge on how any given administration wrote the rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real, growing harm — automated systems making or shaping decisions about jobs, homes, credit, benefits, and liberty with little accountability — and the bill's strongest features (independent audits, a right to a human decision, and court access despite arbitration clauses) are things people cannot currently get in most contexts. The honest costs are real: broad compliance burdens on companies of all sizes, likely higher prices, a thin independent-audit market, and litigation risk from the private right of action. A more careful bill might phase in by company size or risk level; as written, it trades comprehensiveness for administrative weight. The larger problem is that it never advanced at all, so the costs were never weighed by Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it after referral, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act of 2024 in the Senate on September 24, 2024, joined by Senator Mazie Hirono as the bill's only cosponsor [S2][S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that develop and deploy algorithms in hiring, lending, housing, insurance, and other consequential decisions are better off: they face no audit mandates, no disparate-impact liability, no new penalties, and keep forced-arbitration clauses that keep disputes out of court. People subject to automated decisions got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using algorithms in major decisions

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured; the only recorded support was from two Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would impose pre-deployment audits, annual assessments, disclosure duties, and disparate-impact liability on anyone who builds algorithms used in consequential decisions, and would bar the forced-arbitration clauses these companies commonly rely on. It died before any of these costs took effect.

industries.industry: Employers using automated hiring and worker-management tools
industries.note: Employment is the first listed consequential action, so hiring screens, productivity scoring, and termination software would need independent bias audits and would be subject to discrimination suits. Nothing in the record shows these employers weighed in.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, insurers, and landlords using algorithmic decisions
industries.note: Credit, insurance, and housing decisions are all covered; these firms would face audit requirements, state penalties of up to $15,000 per violation or 4% of annual revenue, and private suits. Notably, the bill extends FTC jurisdiction to banks and insurers even where other regulators currently hold it.

The bill would create a legally mandated market: companies could not deploy covered algorithms without independent audits, and the bill would establish a federal occupational series for algorithm auditors. This industry barely exists at scale, which is both an opportunity and a practical bottleneck for the bill's protections.

Platforms are covered when their systems rank or deliver information material to a consequential action (jobs, housing, elections, and similar), but ordinary content ranking outside those areas is untouched. The disclosure and audit duties would still be substantial where the bill applies.
